Question four. What is a confidence interval, really? It's a procedure, not a probability about one interval: the estimate, plus or minus one point nine six standard errors, built on every repeat of an experiment, contains the true value about ninety-five percent of the time. Simulate a hundred test sets for a model that's truly ninety-one percent accurate, and ninety-six of the hundred intervals cover it. Each one either does or doesn't; the ninety-five percent belongs to the procedure. The follow-up is where it breaks. On a slice of forty examples, with a model that's ninety-seven percent right, three slices in ten score forty out of forty, and the textbook interval shrinks to a point. Across all slices, it covers the truth only seventy percent of the time. Wilson's score interval doesn't collapse, and covers ninety-seven.

Question five. What is bootstrapping, and when do you use it? Resample your data with replacement, at its own size, thousands of times, recompute the statistic, and read the interval off the percentiles. No formula needed. Take a thousand simulated request latencies. The ninety-fifth percentile is a hundred and ten milliseconds, and five thousand resamples put it between a hundred and one and a hundred and twenty. The follow-up: resample the unit that was sampled. If two thousand test rows come from two hundred users, resampling rows treats them as independent, and the interval comes out a third too narrow. Resample whole users.
